351.title: The dying man and the fire ordeal (6.15–6.16)
351.hook: a family gathers around a dying man asking, do you know me? then an accused thief is handed a red-hot axe
351.howItsDone: Satya, truthfulness, is counted among the basic virtues in many Hindu ethical lists, including the yamas of the Yoga Sutras, and the Chandogya's closing lessons are often cited when teachers speak of truth as a protection.

segments.voice: Yesterday: acharyavan, the man from Gandhara, untied and pointed home. Your line was someone points the way. Week four of year two begins.

At a deathbed, there's a question families ask. They lean in close, and someone says, gently: do you know me? It's me. For a while the answer is yes, a squeeze of the hand, a name. And then, one day, it isn't. Uddalaka's last two lessons to his son begin at that bedside, and end somewhere very different: in a courtroom, ancient style, with an axe heating in a fire.
screen: `DO YOU KNOW ME? IT'S ME.` → `FOR A WHILE, YES.` → `AN AXE HEATING IN A FIRE.`

segments.voice: First, the bedside. When a man is very ill, Uddalaka says, his relatives gather and ask: do you know me? Do you know me? As long as his speech hasn't gone into his mind, his mind into his breath, his breath into heat, and heat into the highest deity, he knows them. When it has, he doesn't. It's the creation story from ten days ago, running backward: everything folds back, step by step, into Being. Then the second picture, a hard one. In the ancient world, one way to test an accused person was an ordeal. They bring a man with his hands tied. He's taken something, they say. He's a thief. Heat the axe for him. If he did it, he makes himself false. Covering himself with untruth, he grips the hot axe, is burned, and is killed. If he didn't, he makes himself true. Covered with truth, he grips the axe, is not burned, and is set free. Hold this carefully. The Upanishad isn't teaching courtroom procedure, and nobody here is recommending an ordeal. It uses a picture its listeners knew to say one thing: a person wrapped in truth stands on what is real, and the fire can't reach him. A person wrapped in falsehood is standing on nothing. Then, for the last time, the refrain: you are that, Shvetaketu. And the chapter ends with one quiet line: and he understood it. After all his father's pictures, the son gets it.

segments.voice: Notice a few simple true things, I'm breathing, I'm sitting here, my hands are warm or cool, and let each one be solid ground. Then notice anything you've been holding that isn't quite true, a pretense, a small cover story, and without fixing it, feel the difference between standing there and standing on what's true.
Uddalaka, giving his last two lessons to his son. Everything folds back into Being at death, and one covered in truth is not burned.
Your line: truth protects. Tomorrow, a new teacher, and a sage in sorrow. Until then.

352.title: Narada comes to Sanatkumara: "I know the Vedas — I don't know the Self" (7.1)
352.hook: the most learned sage in the room lists everything he has studied, then admits he is still in sorrow
352.howItsDone: Hindu traditions distinguish learning about scripture from knowledge of the self; many teachers quote Narada's confession to students who have studied much and still feel unsettled.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Uddalaka's last lessons, the hot axe, and a son who finally understood. Your line was truth protects.

Every degree on the wall. Diplomas in three languages. A shelf of books with their name on the spine. People call for advice. And one night, the person who owns all of it sits across from a friend and says, quietly: I know all this, and I'm not okay. The seventh chapter of the Chandogya opens with that scene. The man with the diplomas is Narada, a famous sage, and the one he goes to is the sage Sanatkumara.
screen: `EVERY DEGREE ON THE WALL.` → `I KNOW ALL THIS.` → `AND I'M NOT OKAY.`

segments.voice: Teach me, sir, Narada says. Sanatkumara answers: first tell me what you already know, and I'll teach you what's beyond it. So Narada recites his education, and it's long. The Rig Veda, the Yajur Veda, the Sama Veda, the Atharva as the fourth. The old stories and histories as a fifth Veda. Grammar. The rites for the ancestors. Mathematics. The reading of omens. The keeping of time. Logic. Ethics. The science of the gods, of the sacred word, of spirits, of weapons, of the stars, of serpents. Pretty much the whole library of his world. Then the honest sentence the chapter rests on. With all this, sir, I am only a knower of words, not a knower of the self. I have heard from people like you that the knower of the self crosses beyond sorrow: tarati shokam atmavit. And I am in sorrow, sir. Please take me across. He doesn't say his learning was useless. It's real, and it took a lifetime. It just didn't do the one thing he needed. And Sanatkumara's first answer is startling: everything you've studied is only name. Over the next days he'll lead Narada up a ladder, step by step, from name to something greater, and greater again. Uddalaka taught a proud son who thought he knew. Sanatkumara teaches a humble sage who knows he doesn't.

353.title: Name, speech, mind, will, thought — the ladder (7.1–7.5)
353.hook: Narada keeps asking one question, sir, is there anything greater than this? and every time, the answer is yes
353.howItsDone: Teachers of Vedanta often walk students up Sanatkumara's ladder as a contemplative exercise, moving attention from words to mind to awareness.

segments.voice: Yesterday: atmavit, the learned sage who knows words but not the self. Your line was knowledge isn't it.

Kids discover a game early. Why? Because. But why? Because of this. But why that? It drives parents up the wall. And yet it's how you get to the bottom of things: keep asking for the next layer down. Sanatkumara has told Narada that everything he studied is only name. Narada, to his credit, doesn't argue. He asks the next question. Sir, is there anything greater than name?
screen: `WHY? BECAUSE. BUT WHY?` → `ALL YOU KNOW IS ONLY NAME.` → `IS THERE ANYTHING GREATER?`

segments.voice: The first rung is name. Revere name as Brahman, Sanatkumara says. As far as name reaches, you'll have freedom there. A fair start: names are how people hold the world. Is there anything greater than name? Yes, speech. Speech makes the Vedas known, and earth and sky, right and wrong, true and false. Without speech, right and wrong couldn't be made known at all. Greater than speech? Mind. And here's an image from the hand: as a closed fist holds two small fruits, mind holds both speech and name. When you think, let me learn these verses, then you learn them. Let me do this, then you do it. Greater than mind? Will, samkalpa, intention. When you intend something, then you think it, then you say it, then you give it a name. Greater than will? Thought, citta: attention, the awareness that notices before you even intend. And Sanatkumara says something pointed here. If someone knows a great deal but has no real attention, people say: he's nobody. If someone knows little but is truly attentive, people want to listen. Look at the direction of the climb. Name, speech, mind, will, thought. Each rung is quieter and more inward, and each holds the one below it. Narada came in with a mountain of names. Sanatkumara is walking him up and in, toward the one who's paying attention.

354.title: Meditation, understanding, strength, food, water (7.6–7.10)
354.hook: the ladder climbs past thought to meditation, and then takes a surprising turn: toward strength, food and rain
354.howItsDone: Dhyana, meditation, is practiced across Hindu traditions, from Vedanta to yoga, where it is the seventh limb of Patanjali's eight; teachers often describe it with images of stillness like a mountain or a lamp in a windless place.

segments.voice: Yesterday: name, the first rung, then speech, mind, will and thought. Your line was each is greater.

Draw a spiritual ladder, and you'd probably make it climb from the body toward the mind: earthy things at the bottom, airy things at the top. Sanatkumara's ladder starts that way. Name, speech, mind, will, thought, each more inward. Today it reaches meditation, the most inward step yet. And right after that, it does something nobody expects. It climbs toward a strong arm, a meal, and a rain cloud.
screen: `A LADDER FROM BODY TO MIND.` → `TODAY: MEDITATION.` → `THEN A STRONG ARM, A MEAL, A RAIN CLOUD.`

segments.voice: Greater than thought, Sanatkumara says, is meditation, dhyana. The earth meditates, as it were. The sky meditates, as it were. The waters, the mountains, gods and people, all meditate, as it were. Think of a mountain at dusk, utterly still. People who achieve greatness, he adds, seem to have a share of it, while small-minded people are quarrelsome and gossiping. Greater than meditation is understanding, vijnana: by it one knows the Vedas, right and wrong, this world and the next. Then the turn. Greater than understanding is strength. One strong person can make a hundred people of understanding tremble. The earth stands by strength; the mountains stand by it. Greater than strength is food. Go without eating for ten days, and even if you live, you can't see or hear or think or understand. Remember Shvetaketu's fast? Same point. Food returns, and so do they. Greater than food is water. When the rains fail, people grow sick with worry about food; when the rains are good, they're glad. The earth, the sky, the mountains, people, animals, grass and trees, he says, are all water in solid form. So why does the ladder climb into the body? One way to read it: Sanatkumara isn't ranking spirit over matter. He's asking what each thing depends on. Understanding on strength; strength on food; food on rain. The ladder climbs by asking what holds this up.

segments.voice: Let your body settle like rock, heavy and still, held by the ground; a mountain doesn't try. Let the breath move like weather over a peak and thoughts pass like clouds, and just sit, as the earth and the sky and the waters sit, meditating, as it were.
Meditation. Dhyana, the rung above thought: the stillness of earth, sky and mountains. Above it, understanding, strength, food and water.
Your line: the ladder climbs. Tomorrow, the top of it. Day three hundred fifty-four, done.

355.title: Bhuman — the infinite, where one sees nothing else (7.23–7.24)
355.hook: at the top of the ladder Sanatkumara says it plainly: there's no happiness in the small; the infinite is happiness
355.tomorrow: the city of Brahman in the heart
355.howItsDone: Hindu teachers often quote 'the infinite is happiness; there is no happiness in the small' when distinguishing lasting joy from pleasure in possessions, and the bhuma-vidya is a standard topic in Vedanta study.

segments.voice: Yesterday: meditation, then understanding, strength, food and water, a ladder asking what holds each thing up. Your line was the ladder climbs.

A kid swimming far out on a summer afternoon. Friends at a table late at night, laughing until it hurts. A parent holding a newborn at 3am. Some people say afterward that in moments like these there was no thought of being happy. No one over here, and happiness over there. Just the thing itself. Sanatkumara's ladder, after many rungs, arrives at something like that, and gives it a name.
screen: `NO THOUGHT OF BEING HAPPY.` → `NO ONE OVER HERE.` → `JUST THE THING ITSELF.`

segments.voice: Between yesterday and today, the ladder climbs through heat, space, memory, hope and breath, then turns toward truth, understanding, thinking, faith, steadfastness and action. At the top, Sanatkumara says: a person acts only when they find happiness. So, Narada, you should want to understand happiness. Then the line at the heart of the chapter. Yo vai bhuma tat sukham, nalpe sukham asti. The infinite is happiness. There is no happiness in the small. Bhuma means the vast, the full, the unbounded. Alpa means the small, the limited. Here's how to tell them apart: where one sees nothing else, hears nothing else, understands nothing else, that is the infinite. Where one sees, hears, understands something else, that is the small. Think back to the ocean, the laughter, the newborn: nothing else, for a moment. A taste of what he means. Narada asks: but sir, what does the infinite rest on? On its own greatness, Sanatkumara says. Or, not even on greatness. People here call cows and horses greatness, and elephants and gold, servants and spouses, fields and houses. I don't mean that. Those things rest on something else. The infinite rests on nothing. It's above and below, east and west, everywhere. And then: I am all this. The self is all this. The chapter ends quietly: Sanatkumara showed Narada the far shore beyond darkness.

356.title: The city of Brahman in the heart (8.1)
356.hook: inside the body is a small lotus-shaped house, and inside that a small space, as big as all the space outside
356.tomorrow: Indra and Virochana learn from Prajapati
356.howItsDone: Meditation on the space in the heart, the dahara-vidya, is taught in several Hindu traditions, and many devotional schools picture God dwelling in the lotus of the heart.

segments.voice: Yesterday: bhuman, the infinite, where one sees nothing else. Your line was the infinite is happiness.

Russian nesting dolls get smaller as you go in. Open the big one, and there's a smaller one; open that, smaller again, until a tiny solid doll the size of a bean. The last chapter of the Chandogya opens with a nesting picture too: a city, a house, a room. Only this one does the opposite. The farther in you go, the bigger it gets.
screen: `NESTING DOLLS, SMALLER EACH TIME.` → `A CITY, A HOUSE, A ROOM.` → `THE FARTHER IN, THE BIGGER.`

segments.voice: In this city of Brahman, the eighth chapter begins, there is a small house shaped like a lotus, and inside it a small space. What is inside that space should be sought, and understood. The city of Brahman is the body. The lotus-shaped house is the heart. And the small space is, well, small. So the students ask the obvious question. A tiny space in a tiny house in this body: what could be in there worth looking for? The teacher answers: as large as this space out here is, that large is the space within the heart. Both heaven and earth are contained in it. Fire and wind, sun and moon, lightning and stars. Whatever there is here, and whatever there isn't, all of it is held there. The students push again, and it's a good question. If everything is held inside this body, what's left when the body grows old, or dies? The answer: that doesn't grow old when the body grows old. It isn't killed when the body is killed. That is the real city of Brahman. And the text describes that inner self: free from evil, from old age, from death, from grief, from hunger and thirst. Its desires are true. Its intentions are true. Remember Satyakama, the boy who loves truth? Here the same word, satyakama, describes the self in every heart. So the nesting dolls run backward: body, heart, a small space, and inside the small space, everything.

segments.voice: Breathe into the center of your chest and imagine a small, quiet space there, like the inside of a closed flower. Then, on each breath out, let it open gently, wider than your chest, wider than the room, as wide as the sky, with sun, moon and stars held inside it.
Dahara, small, subtle. The body is the city, the heart a lotus-shaped house, and the small space inside holds heaven and earth.

357.title: Indra and Virochana learn from Prajapati — the body is not the self (8.7–8.8)
357.hook: a god and a demon study for thirty-two years, are told to look in a pan of water, and both walk away thinking the reflection is the self
357.howItsDone: Vedanta teachers often use the story of Indra and Virochana to introduce the difference between the body and the self, and the story's stages are read as a step-by-step inquiry into who we are.

segments.voice: Yesterday: dahara, a small space as large as all space. Your line was the space in the heart. Today ends week four of year two.

A mirror by the front door. Good shirt. Hair right. That's me, says the glance, before any thought. Then a selfie: me again. Then a tagged photo from ten years ago: somehow, also me. People point at a lot of pictures and say me. The Chandogya tells of two students who did exactly that, and one of them took the mistake home and built a whole philosophy on it.
screen: `GOOD SHIRT. HAIR RIGHT.` → `THAT'S ME.` → `WE POINT AT PICTURES AND SAY ME.`

segments.voice: Prajapati, the lord of creatures, announces: there is a self free from evil, from old age and death, from grief, hunger and thirst. Whoever finds it gains all worlds. The gods and the demons both hear. The gods send their king, Indra. The demons send theirs, Virochana. The two rivals arrive with firewood in their hands, not speaking to each other, and live as students for thirty-two years. Then Prajapati teaches: the person seen in the eye, that is the self. Immortal, fearless. That is Brahman. They ask: and the one seen in water, or in a mirror? It's seen in all these, he says. Look at yourselves in a pan of water. What do you see? Our whole selves, sir, down to the hair and the nails. Now dress up well, put on ornaments, and look again. Just as we are, sir, well dressed and adorned, so are these two. That is the self, says Prajapati, immortal, fearless. Both leave content. Prajapati watches them go: they go without having found the self. Shankara and other commentators say he meant the seer behind the eye, and the students heard the image in the eye. Virochana goes home and teaches the demons that the body is the self: honor it, adorn it, serve it. Indra sets off too, but on the road, something starts to bother him. This week, from the top: truth protects. Narada, a knower of words. The ladder, from name up to rain. The infinite. The space in the heart. And today, two students mistaking the reflection for the one who sees.
screen: `A SELF FREE FROM DEATH AND GRIEF.` · `THIRTY-TWO YEARS AS STUDENTS.` · `LOOK IN A PAN OF WATER.` · `THE WEEK, FROM THE TOP.` · then, large: `THE REFLECTION ISN'T YOU.`

segments.voice: Picture your face in a mirror, clearly, and then ask gently: who's looking? Don't answer with words; turn your attention back toward the looking itself, like turning around in a doorway, and each time you drift back to the picture, turn around again.
Prajapati, lord of creatures. A god and a demon look in a pan of water, adorned, and both mistake the reflection for the self Prajapati described.
Your line: the reflection isn't you. On the road, Indra isn't so sure. Week four of year two, done.
